en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Puṇyabala,
Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Shi Hu, et al., in obedience to the Imperial Decree.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and went to the Andhavana forest; beneath a certain tree, he stayed for the day, sitting in tranquil seclusion.

At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus gathered separately in a hall within the grove and sat down in order. These included the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Śata-bhūmi, the Venerable Aniruddha, and the Venerable Śāriputra. Once this assembly of bhikṣus had gathered together, they said to one another:
"What practice do people of the world engage in that yields the greatest benefit?"
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"If a person practices the cultivation of the characteristics of form and their activities, they will obtain much benefit.
The Venerable Śrutaviṃśatikoṭi said:
"Regarding the practice of diligent application, if a person cultivates it,
they will obtain much benefit. Venerable Aniruddha said,
"Regarding the practice of craftsmanship, if a person cultivates it, they will obtain much benefit."
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
"If a person practices the activities of wisdom, they will obtain much benefit and profit.
Having spoken thus, they all thought to themselves:
"Our current discourse differs and is not uniform, as each of us establishes what is supreme for ourselves.
If we were to go and question the World-Honored One regarding this matter, he would surely preach to us according to our respective needs."
As you have taught, we shall uphold it. Why is this?
Because the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, is able to sever our doubts; he is one of great compassion.
Just as the sunlight illuminates all darkness, one uses all-encompassing wisdom to shatter all doubts;
one unties the net of suffering to rescue sentient beings, leading them back to the right path;
and one regards all sentient beings with equality, as if they were one's only child.
He has attained mastery over all phenomena;
through all phenomena, he brings about great benefit.
The Great Muni is able to pacify all doubts for all beings.
"The Buddha constantly and diligently works to untie the knots of doubt; therefore, we should go together to question him.
After the bhikṣus had thus deliberated with one another, they desired to go and see the Buddha.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was in the forest, he heard with his pure divine ear—surpassing that of humans—the bhikṣu saṃgha gathered together to discuss such matters. He immediately arose from samādhi and went to where the bhikṣus were.
Then the bhikṣus went forward to welcome the World-Honored One, prepared seats, and invited him to be seated.
Once the Buddha had taken his seat, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!"
I have just heard you all deliberating among yourselves, saying:
"Among the people of the world, what practice brings the greatest benefit?
First, Ānanda said that the cultivation of physical form (*rūpa*) brings great benefit.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said that through diligent practice one gains much benefit;
Aniruddha said that through skillful practice one gains much benefit;
Śāriputra said that through the practice of wisdom one gains much benefit.
Having spoken thus, he further gave rise to this thought:
"The distinctions that have been explained are not equal, for each has established its own as supreme."
"If we were to go and ask the World-Honored One about this matter, he would surely explain it to us according to what is appropriate.
We would then uphold it exactly as he has spoken.
What do you think of this?
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“Truly so, World-Honored One!”
"We have recently gathered for discussion on this very matter; we pray that the Buddha will now resolve our doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to give rise to this occasion, spoke these verses:
"Physical form, skillfulness, and diligence— Among these, wisdom is the most supreme."
"If sentient beings cultivate the causes of merit, the fruits of merit they obtain will be even more supreme.
Having spoken these verses, he further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus, there may be times when a person practices with respect to form and other characteristics; yet, this does not yield great benefit in every way or at all times."
If one cultivates the power of merit, one will obtain great benefit in every way and at all times. O Bhikṣus!
Among all dharmas, I do not see a single one through which sentient beings, having practiced it accordingly, obtain as much benefit as they do through the power of merit.
For what reason? O Bhikṣus!

I recall that in a past life there was a king named Netra-bala, who resided in a royal city. He administered state affairs well, possessed vast majesty and spiritual power, and his realm was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with a flourishing population.
That king had a queen named Guangzhao (Universal Radiance), whose physical form was exceptionally sublime and whom all people delighted to behold.

At one time, Queen Guangzhao gathered with the king for a meeting, engaging in play and amusement. Due to that joyful diversion, she gave birth to a son whose deportment was dignified and upright, whom all people delighted to behold; he was more sublime than ordinary men and possessed the physical marks of a celestial being.

Furthermore, that prince has, from birth, extensively planted the causes for excellent physical marks; because he is endowed with such exquisite and sublime features, he is therefore now named Varṇabalā.
In this manner, in succession, three sons were subsequently born to him:
the first was endowed with diligence, the second with skill in the arts, and the third with wisdom.
"Furthermore, monks!
That Queen Vistara-prabhā was again to conceive her final child. On that very day, various kinds of precious jewels suddenly descended from the heavens into the royal palace;
furthermore, exquisite and diverse jeweled ornaments and canopies appeared simultaneously, covering the queen."
At that time, King Cakṣu-bala, having witnessed this rare and extraordinary event, was struck with wonder in his heart;
he immediately summoned the physiognomists and questioned them, saying:
"What is the cause of these rare and extraordinary signs?"
The physiognomist replied:

"Great King, you should know that the Queen has conceived a child within her sacred womb; this child possesses great merit and is endowed with great majesty and virtue, and shall attain a renowned name."
Upon hearing these words, the king was again filled with wonder and admiration. Later, Queen Viśākhā suddenly gave rise to a thought and spoke thus:
"How great! How marvelous!"
"I now wish to mount the most excellent lion throne, covered with a white parasol and attended by a precious fly-whisk.
He then reported these matters in detail to the king.

Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy; he issued an edict to thoroughly purify and adorn the interior and exterior of the palace, and had everything prepared exactly as desired.
"Furthermore, at one time, Queen Vistīrṇaprabhā suddenly gave rise to a thought and spoke these words:

'I shall now go to that great heap of gold and jewels, sit upon it, and at will raise my hand to take gold and jewels for myself, and extensively practice giving for the sake of all beings, so that those who are destitute may have their wealth and treasures made abundant.'"
He reported the matter to the king, and the king acted accordingly.
"Furthermore, on another occasion, Queen Vistīrṇaprabhā suddenly gave rise to a thought and spoke these words:
'How wonderful!'"
"I now wish to release all those who are imprisoned and bound.
Having reported this matter to the king, the king, according to his desire, issued a decree to both the inner and outer courts to release all prisoners.
"Furthermore, at one time, Queen Viśākhā suddenly gave rise to a thought and spoke these words:
'How wonderful!
I now wish to roam through the gardens and groves.'"
The matter was reported to the king, who, according to her wish, had the gardens cleaned for her to enjoy.
Furthermore, at another time, Queen Viśākhā suddenly felt a thought arise and spoke these words:
"How wonderful!"
Now, before this great assembly of my retinue in this palace, I utter these words of truth:
"If I truly possess meritorious rewards, may the devas and humans swiftly present me with a most exquisite and magnificent lion throne."
"Once I have attained it and taken my place upon that seat, I shall extensively proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for the multitudes.
Having spoken thus, he waited expectantly for the various devas to manifest rare and wondrous signs.

When the King was informed of these matters, King Cakṣu immediately issued orders throughout his palace to ensure that the entire city, both inside and out, was thoroughly cleansed and purified. All the people were commanded to don clean garments and exquisite ornaments, each carrying various fragrances and flower garlands, and they all gathered together.

At that time, Queen Guangzhao, adorned with a multitude of exquisite ornaments and surrounded by palace ladies, kinsmen, and attendants, went forth before the assembly. Her physical marks were so majestic that she resembled a celestial maiden;
all the people gazed upon her, and they were filled with joy.
At that time, the queen, having conceived a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, looked up into the sky and, through the power of her true resolve, spoke this verse:
“If the power of these three blessings—of the Lord of Heaven, the Lord of Men, and Liberation—is supreme;
by the force of this truth, at this very moment, may the heavens swiftly spread out the lion throne.”
"Having spoken these verses, immediately and suddenly, excellent and wondrous lion-thrones descended from the heavens, and exquisite flowers were scattered;
all the devas in the sky were filled with joy."
At that time, when the multitude of people saw this rare and extraordinary event, they all felt love and joy, and together they marveled at it, speaking these verses:
“Rare indeed is his great merit and mighty power; The entire world now makes offerings to him.
What humans desire, the gods can fulfill; The power of those gods’ merit is supreme.”
At that time, Queen Guangzhao (Vipulaprabhā) felt great joy in her heart and took her place upon the lion throne.

As soon as she had ascended it, the great earth shook in six ways; the lion throne then rose up from the ground and hovered in mid-air at a height of seven human spans. It was further adorned with various kinds of exquisite and rare jewels, and a canopy of precious drapery covered the seat.

When those multitudes of people saw these extraordinary and marvelous signs of the power of merit, they conceived a sense of joy and delight. Each offered the various fragrant flowers and garlands they held to the Queen; with palms joined in solemn reverence and a mind intent on benefit, they sat before her to listen to her words.
At that time, King Cakṣuśīla, having witnessed this event, was filled with supreme joy; together with his ministers and retinue, he joined his palms in solemn reverence and sat down in order.
At that time, Queen Viśālanetrā spoke these verses:
“Human beings should cultivate all causes of merit, Acting as they have done, without interruption;
When they practice according to their aspirations, They shall obtain sublime bliss by virtue of that treasury of merit.”
After these verses had been spoken, a voice spontaneously arose in the air, praising him:
"You have now spoken well!
You have spoken most excellently!"
Furthermore, from the sky, subtle and lovely celestial music was played.

As King Akṣimat and the multitude heard these verses being recited, exquisite garments and ornaments spontaneously descended from the heavens, each falling upon their bodies. The king and the multitude immediately took the garments and ornaments that had fallen and presented them before the queen, praising her with one voice:
"Excellent teaching!"
"Excellent teaching!
At that moment, the Queen descended slowly from the lion throne through the air and settled safely upon the ground.
Thereupon, the celestial music immediately ceased, and the music of the human world was played once more; the King and the assembled multitude all felt profound reverence.
Having made extensive offerings, everyone was filled with joy.
Then, Queen Guangzhao returned to the palace; once she had entered, that lion throne vanished from mid-air.
At that time, the multitude of people clearly beheld the aforementioned auspicious signs and, filled with joy, exclaimed in praise:
"How marvelous is the power of merit! You possess such great majesty and virtue."
"How marvelous is the power of merit; this is its sweet fruit!
At that time, Queen Guangzhao, while dwelling within the palace, ceased all her activities and thoughts;

thereafter, when ten months had been fulfilled, at the moment the sun first rose, she gave birth to a crown prince whose physical appearance was upright and majestic, a sight that all people delighted to behold.
Immediately, the great earth shook in six ways;
within his palace, the seven precious jewels rained down naturally from the sky;
and throughout all places inside and outside the royal city, there fell various kinds of celestial, wondrous garments, as well as the most excellent and pleasing exquisite flowers.
Everywhere, all the flowering trees and fruit trees were in full bloom and laden with fruit;
a fine, sweet rain fell in gentle drizzles everywhere;
and from the four directions, a mild and harmonious breeze arose slowly.
Once the Prince was born, he was placed securely upon the ground;

immediately, by the majestic spiritual power of the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the earth suddenly split open, and a magnificent lion throne, adorned with various exquisite jewels, surged forth from within to be offered to the Prince.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, held a celestial, exquisite parasol and various precious fly-whisks to cover him from above.

The hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down celestial, exquisite garments and jeweled canopies; they also rained down various kinds of rare jewels, or ornaments, or exquisite robes and decorations, or celestial, exquisite flowers, or powdered incense, unguents, and flower garlands; or there were celestial musical instruments producing the sounds of exquisite songs.

By the divine power of the devaputra Viśvakarman, all thorns and gravel were removed from within and without the royal city; it was spread with silken fabrics and adorned with strings of pearls. Sublime banners and pennants made of various jewels were erected, and pure sandalwood perfumed water was sprinkled everywhere. Exquisite incense jars were placed all around, various flowers were scattered, and every kind of pleasing arrangement was provided.
Furthermore, one hundred great elephants came spontaneously from the wilderness and entered the royal palace, staying in the stables.
Additionally, one hundred oxen came to the fields; without the need for plowing or sowing, all seeds ripened fully and naturally according to the seasons.

"Furthermore, beneath that lion throne, there are five great treasuries filled with various jewels; their doors are opened wide, and one may take from them as needed for use, yet they can never be exhausted."
Furthermore, at that time, all hostile sentient beings, in an instant, turned toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness.
Then the Prince, by the power of his past lives, his supernormal knowledges, and his majestic virtue, immediately upon birth, surveyed the four directions and spoke these verses:
"Human beings should cultivate the causes of all merit; As they have been performed, let them not be interrupted."
"When acting according to one's desires, one attains sublime joy by virtue of the treasury of merit.

At that time, another class of devas in the sky, having witnessed this vast and wondrous display of supernormal power, majestic virtue, and extraordinary, unique force of merit, were all filled with joy and felt deep affection for it. To inspire the power of merit in him, they spoke these verses:
"The sons of the gods in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, And the lords of the palace in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,"
"The power of those merits is most lovely; seeing this superior merit, one rejoices all the more.

At that time, King Cakṣuṣmat, together with his palace ladies, attendants, retinue, and elder ministers, clearly beheld such auspicious and excellent signs; they were all filled with wonder and admiration, and spoke these words:
"How marvelous!"
The Prince possesses great power of merit.
How marvelous!
The Prince is endowed with great renown.
"Now that I have been born among humans, such auspicious, vast, and supreme signs as these have appeared simultaneously in the midst of the heavens.
At that time, the king was filled with joy; out of affection for his son, he commanded the treasurer:

"You must now open my treasuries and bring forth all the gold and jewels therein. I shall bestow them upon those who offer virtuous benedictions, so that they may all obtain abundant wealth and riches, and that they may offer me excellent praises and perform extensive meritorious deeds."
"Furthermore, I pray that through the vast accumulation of auspicious and supreme merit throughout my successive lives, I may establish a name for this prince.
He then immediately addressed his ministers and assistants, saying,
"What name should now be given to this prince?"
The close attendants addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
Now this prince has manifested at birth many auspicious signs of superior power and merit; therefore, it is fitting that he be named Puṇyabala."
Immediately, the king commanded that Puṇyabala be given his name.
At that time, the king entrusted Prince Puṇyabala to eight nurses:
two to carry him, two to suckle him, two to wash and bathe him, and two to play with him.

May those eight nurses provide nourishment, suckle, bathe, and play with him at the proper times; may they supply all other excellent articles of enjoyment so that he may have abundant provisions for his use, and may he grow up quickly, like a pure lotus in a pond.

Thereafter, when the prince had gradually grown up, he studied various scripts; as soon as he studied them, he was able to exhaustively master their profound subtleties. Among the Kṣatriya royal lineage, he attained complete mastery in all subjects worthy of study.

That crown prince, possessing deep faith in the virtuous and good, with a pure inner mind, performed all his actions for the benefit of both himself and others; he was one endowed with compassion and pity.

Possessing mastery over all phenomena, he compassionately rescues sentient beings; he practices various forms of giving without accumulating anything, able to relinquish everything—giving extensively and giving universally, such that there is not the slightest thing he does not give away.

That is to say, if there were śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, the poor, the destitute, or beggars who came seeking the flesh and blood of his own body, at that time the Prince would immediately give rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward those beggars and regard them as being like space, thinking to himself:
"How wonderful!"

I shall now cause those who beg to have their wishes fulfilled; I will grant them immediately. How much more so for all my gold, silver, and precious jewels, food, drink, clothing, ointments, flower garlands, various bedding and furniture, as well as other desired articles of enjoyment—I pray that all these may appear at the mere thought of them, so that having obtained them, I may bestow them upon all seekers and cause their intentions and desires to be entirely fulfilled.
Because the Prince possessed these virtues, his fame spread throughout Jambudvīpa, reaching down to the realm of the nāgas and up to the Brahma heavens, being heard everywhere.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Puṇyabala Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Puṇyabala Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Meritorious Servant, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Purple-robed Śramaṇa Subject Shi Hu and others, by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, at a later time, Prince Puṇyabala went out to the park with his four elder brothers.

On the way, there were thousands upon thousands of needle-mouthed *preta*s dwelling on the mid-slope of a mountain; their forms were emaciated like heaps of bones, and their entire bodies were ablaze with fire. A host of ghosts surrounded them, invisible to all people except for Prince Puṇyabala, who first beheld their condition."
Then that hungry ghost, joining his palms before him, addressed the prince, saying:
"You possess great merit and vast renown; you are one who is compassionate."
"We are tormented by hunger and thirst and oppressed by suffering; we pray that you will now grant us a small portion of food and drink.

Because we created causes of stinginess in past lives, we have fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts in this life. For countless thousands of years, we have not obtained water to drink, let alone being able to see any food."
At that time, Prince Puṇyabala looked up into the sky and immediately gave rise to a compassionate thought:
"How wonderful!
If I could now obtain even a small portion of food and drink sent down from heaven, I would use it to provide sustenance for this multitude of hungry ghosts."
At that moment, a great quantity of food and drink suddenly descended from the heavens.
Prince Puṇyabala immediately used this food to provide sustenance for the hungry ghosts.
Due to the power of their past karma, that host of hungry ghosts could not see him at all, and they all spoke these words:
"O Prince! We have heard in the past that you are one who possesses compassion; why is it that at this time you do not provide us with food and drink?"
The Prince said:
"I have brought down food and drink from the heavens and previously offered it to you; why do you not take it now?
The hungry ghosts replied:
“‘Prince! Due to the power of our past karma, none of us are able to see.
At that time, Prince Puṇyabala again had this thought:”
"How pitiable!
This stinginess is truly unlovely.
Thus he spoke these words:
"If these meritorious rewards possess great power, by virtue of my words of truth, may this hungry ghost be able to see food and drink, so that it may partake of them all according to its needs."
Having spoken these words, all those hungry ghosts were suddenly able to see the food; their appearances immediately transformed, and their faces became like those of humans.
Prince Puṇyabala felt great joy in his heart and proceeded to let them take as much food and drink as they desired.

Once that host of hungry ghosts had obtained food, their hunger and thirst were instantly stilled; their physical strength was fully restored, they became robust and flourishing, and their forms were no longer hideous. They then conceived pure and joyful thoughts toward Prince Puṇyabala.
Immediately they passed away and were all reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. Floating in mid-air, they addressed the prince, saying: "Prince!..."
‘That we have been born in the Tuṣita Heaven is entirely due to the majestic power established by you.

Having heard these wondrous and virtuous words, Prince Puṇyabala was deeply and greatly delighted; he immediately proceeded forward to the grove and held a consultation with his elder brothers, saying:
‘What practice should the people of the world undertake to obtain the greatest benefit?’
The one endowed with the perfection of physical form said:
"In this world, regarding the practice of physical forms and actions, if a person cultivates them, they will obtain much benefit and profit.
How is this known?"
That is to say, if there is someone whom others have not seen before, they rejoice upon seeing them;
those who previously did not hold them in high esteem, come to hold them in high esteem after seeing them.

As my venerable teacher, the Rishi, also said in the past: "If one is endowed with excellent physical marks, one will be pleasing to others; that exquisite form is worth beholding, and all will look upon it with reverence, love, and delight."
"It is just as a wise person who delights in the supreme Dharma and provides all manner of offerings.
Furthermore, those endowed with diligence said:
"It is not by cultivating physical marks that one gains great benefit!"
Now, this should be understood: if a person practices the activity of diligent application, they will obtain great benefit. Why is this?
For even if one cultivates physical form, if there is no diligence, how could one possibly obtain desirable fruits in both the present life and future lives?
If some claim that those who obtain many benefits through physical forms are wise, they are actually fools, shrouded by deluded views.

As I have taught, regarding the practice of diligent application that can achieve desirable fruits in the present life: this refers to how a farmer plants seeds, a merchant gains profit, an official receives a salary, a student masters the teachings, and one practicing meditative concentration attains the fruit of pliancy—all of which are the various desirable fruits accomplished through diligence in the present life.

Furthermore, regarding this diligence that can produce desirable fruits in future lives—namely, birth in the higher realms, birth in the celestial worlds, great wealth and sovereignty, and the direct realization of liberation—all these are the desirable fruits accomplished by diligence in future lives.
All these virtues rely upon diligence as their foundation.
Furthermore, this diligence can remedy timidity and weakness; if one applies diligence, there is not the slightest phenomenon that cannot be accomplished.
"Furthermore, the one perfected in arts said:
'O worthy sirs, although you have spoken in many ways, you truly cannot satisfy my mind.'"
Why is this? For all forms of diligence, if they lack skillful means (*upāya*), they can never result in any manifest accomplishment;
however, if diligence is joined with skillful means, then that which is undertaken will be accomplished in accordance with reality.
Therefore, one should know that if a person practices the craft of artisanry, they will obtain great benefit and profit.

Furthermore, those possessed of such skillfulness—whether kings, ministers, śramaṇas, brahmins, householders, or even those of low birth, as well as other artisans—all come to offer their services and gifts.
"Furthermore, those endowed with wisdom say:
'You should know that when people practice and achieve great benefit and profit, it is neither due to physical appearance, nor diligence, nor skillful craft.'"
Why is this? If there is no wisdom regarding the forms and characteristics being observed, although they may appear similar, they will not be pure or sublime.
If there is no wisdom regarding the diligence that is initiated, although one may attain benefit and profit, nothing will be accomplished.
Regarding the various crafts and skills one performs, if one lacks wisdom, even though one may engage in their cultivation, one will be unable to master or maintain them.
Therefore, one should know that wisdom can accomplish all undertakings; if a person practices and acts with it, they will obtain great benefit and profit.
"Furthermore, this wisdom can attain physical forms, accomplish crafts and skills, inspire diligence, and procure all the sublime pleasures among human beings.
At that time, Prince Puṇyabala gazed upon the one possessed of wisdom with a joyful countenance and said to him: "So it is, so it is!
What you have said is true.
All physical forms, crafts, and diligence cannot yield great benefit if they lack wisdom.
Therefore, one should know that wisdom is universally capable of sustaining all fruits that accord with reality.
"O Benevolent One!
However, if this wisdom lacks the power of merit, whatever one undertakes will not be accomplished.
Therefore, know truly that if a person cultivates merit, they will obtain many benefits and advantages."
Why is this? Merit is a fruit that is purely singular; merit is a fruit of radiance; merit is a fruit that is pleasing to the mind; merit is a fruit of satisfaction.
Such fruits of merit—I cannot fully describe their virtues. Now, for the sake of awakening you all, I shall speak of but a small portion from among the gates of merit; listen well.

By virtue of merit, one obtains a beautiful physical form; merit is endowed with diligence; through merit one attains auspiciousness as well as great wealth; merit is endowed with wisdom; merit enables one to sing the praises of the virtues of the True Dharma; merit is endowed with sharp intelligence; merit leads one to walk the Right Path; merit causes birth into a noble lineage; merit grants the recollection of past lives; merit is endowed with renown; merit perfects the practice of ethical discipline; merit enables one to practice generosity; by the power of merit, one’s faculties always remain unimpaired; merit brings constant happiness; one who possesses merit is always honored by the wise; merit perfects all powers; and by the power of merit, one always encounters virtuous friends and spiritual teachers. Furthermore, the power of merit enables the accomplishment of all undertakings—whether it be farming the fields or engaging in commerce to seek profit—one achieves vast accumulation with little effort, becoming wealthy, prosperous, and independent.

Possessing merit, they are able to have their clothing, food, drink, and precious treasures naturally rain down from the void during the mere thought of them; everything being fully provided, they experience happiness accordingly.
Through merit, one obtains a pleasing and excellent dwelling;
through merit, in both the present life and future births, one constantly gains beautiful wives, daughters, retinues, wealth, grain, and so forth.
The ground traversed by those of merit naturally becomes free of thorns and gravel, remaining level and stable;
those of merit also obtain a vast and majestic physical form;
and if there is a person afflicted by illness, when touched by the hand of one with merit, the disease is immediately alleviated and cured.
Furthermore, merit follows those who possess it; it can produce food, drink, clothing, precious jewels, wealth, and grain, providing inexhaustible resources for their use.
Those with merit are constantly protected by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, and others in every place, just as the deity who protects the crops does during the rainy season.
One who possesses merit is always respected and cherished by many;
merit brings a good reputation, and merit is praised by others.
Through merit, one is always able to be endowed with all the factors of wholesome dharmas.
Those with merit are trusted and followed by others in their speech;
those with merit always possess a radiant and lovely luster;
those with merit always produce the subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice.
One who possesses merit has limbs that are naturally supple;
one who possesses merit always utters wondrous and virtuous speech;
one who possesses merit always encounters good friends and wise people, and does not have their retinue destroyed.
The meritorious are free from illness;
the meritorious are beloved by others;
the meritorious obtain wealth and profit.
Merit is valorous.
Furthermore, one of great merit becomes a king of men, possessing everything without exception and free from all diseases;
merit ensures that one always attains abundant prosperity that is never destroyed.
One who possesses merit obtains the treasure-store of a wheel-turning monarch, complete with the seven jewels;
one who possesses merit is able to travel through the void;
one who possesses merit has majestic radiance equal to that of the sun and moon.
Through merit one becomes the Moon Deity;
through merit one becomes the Sun Deity;
through merit one becomes Brahmā, King of the Gods.
One with merit becomes Śakra;
one with merit can traverse the palatial towers of the celestial mansions like those gods;
one with merit possesses great power and majesty like the asura kings.
Those with merit are always born in the happy realms;
those with merit abandon the miserable realms;
and those with merit constantly obtain exquisite, pleasing, and wondrous flowers that are most difficult to find.
Those with merit achieve success in all their undertakings;
those with merit are able to provide illumination for the world;
and those with merit constantly receive the offerings and sincere faith of devas, humans, asuras, and others.
"When the Prince spoke of these various meritorious deeds, his four elder brothers held different views and their practices were not the same. Thereupon, the Prince spoke again, saying:
'I now wish to go secretly with my brothers to another country; wherever we may dwell, we shall verify these matters.'"
"Should those with physical beauty practice more?
Or should those with diligence, craftsmanship, wisdom, or the power of merit practice more?
When the four elder brothers heard these words, they each followed their own inclinations and no longer informed their father the king, immediately departing for other lands.
“Having entered a country, they changed their attire and each sought a place to settle.

At that time, those endowed with beautiful physical forms, because of their exquisite appearance, were gazed upon by people who all felt joy; consequently, they obtained great wealth and enjoyed abundant provisions.”
One who is endowed with diligence, by virtue of their heroic strength, is able to take hold of something;

yet suddenly they see a great river of swift current, deep and wide, and terrifying. Within it stands a massive sandalwood tree. That diligent person takes hold of that tree, trades it for profit, and thereby becomes wealthy and prosperous, enjoying and sustaining themselves with its resources.
One who is endowed with skillful arts, through the power of those arts, performs various tasks; by thereby attaining great wealth, they enjoy the means of sustenance.

One who is endowed with wisdom, because of their clever intelligence, is able to overcome powerful enemies and further manages to associate with those possessing wealth and power; by pleasing them and causing them joy, they obtain clothing, ornaments, and treasures as they desire, and thus enjoy the means of sustenance according to their happiness.
"At that time, Prince Puṇyabala, by virtue of his own supreme merit and the power of his great majesty, traveled everywhere performing acts of benefit and meritorious deeds.

One day, he happened to pass by the house of a poor man and entered it; through the power of the prince’s merit, auspicious and magnificent signs suddenly appeared within that dwelling, and it became filled to the brim with gold, jewels, wealth, and grain."
At that time, the poor man, having seen this, was struck with wonder and joy, and thought to himself:
"Such a thing as this has never occurred before; from what cause does it arise?"
"From where has this come?
Is it not that this person came into my house, and was it due to his power that this occurred?
He further thought:

"In the past, I suffered extreme poverty, but now I have attained victory and all things are abundant; this must surely be due to this person coming here, causing auspicious signs to appear within my home."
"This person possesses great merit and has a vast reputation; it is fitting that we should honor and make offerings to him with respect.
Consequently, they venerated him continuously and without interruption.
The Prince brought great wealth and prosperity to that poor man’s house and made him happy; subsequently, his fame spread everywhere:
"In such-and-such a house, which was formerly extremely destitute, a certain extraordinary person entered; by his power, auspicious signs suddenly appeared in that house."
Upon hearing this, all the people conceived deep faith and reverence for Prince Puṇyabala, and together they praised him, saying:
"How marvelous!
Such supreme merit possesses such great power!"

Furthermore, by the power of the Prince’s merit, in that region the flowering and fruit-bearing trees blossomed and bore fruit; the seasons did not fail, sweet rain fell everywhere, and seeds sprouted and grew to become lush and flourishing.
At that time, the multitude of people felt deep affection and joy for Prince Puṇyabala and all came together to behold him.
Then the prince, in order to universally gather the minds of those who had come, formed this thought:
"How wonderful! How delightful!"

At this time, within my home, it is possible to obtain all manner of precious jewels, various articles of enjoyment, and other exquisite, skillfully crafted, and pleasing objects, so that those who come may be provided with everything they need.
When he gave rise to this thought, all manner of precious treasures and the like appeared instantly as he had intended, all of them abundant and overflowing.
At that time, the multitude of people, struck with wonder and amazement, exclaimed: "How marvelous!"
"Great merit results in sweet fruit.
Thus, they all conceived a sense of reverence for the Prince.

At that time, the Prince, according to what was appropriate for each person, gathered them together through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) with impartiality, bringing them all into harmony; namely, by sharing equally in giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
Consequently, his fame spread throughout all kingdoms, cities, and villages.

Later, at one point, the prince gradually arrived at a certain kingdom where he saw the king punishing a man who was a skilled physician; the king had commanded the prison official to dismember him, severing his limbs and cutting off his hands and feet.
With much blood flowing and suffering the agony of intense torment, the person being punished, upon seeing the Prince, let out a great cry of distress and wept, saying:
"O Benevolent One!..."
Save me, O Benevolent One! Save me!
At that moment, the Prince was deeply moved by this matter and reflected to himself:
"By what skillful means can I now rescue this person from their suffering?
While he was thus reflecting, a sudden insight arose within him: "The power of merit gained through the performance of giving, as it exists in me, is visible to the world."

Having formed this thought, his compassionate heart was stirred within; he immediately tore open his own body, drew forth much blood, and gave it to the other to drink, whereby their suffering and affliction were removed.

Seeing that the man’s hands and feet had already been severed and that he was in extreme agony, the Prince immediately took a sharp blade, cut off his own hands and feet, and placed them upon the places where the man’s hands and feet had been severed.
At that time, the Prince surveyed the sky and, extending a mind of universal compassion toward all sentient beings, made this vast and true vow:

"In this life, I have never committed even the slightest unwholesome deed; if what I have spoken is true, may the hands and feet of this person, severed from their limbs, be rejoined at this very moment, restored exactly as they were before."
Having spoken these words, that person’s limbs and joints immediately joined together; his body was restored in its entirety, returning to its former state as it had been.
Upon seeing this, the Prince’s aspiration was fulfilled, and he thought to himself:
"Through my diligent effort, what I set out to do has been accomplished; by shedding my own blood, I have rescued this man from his suffering."
He severed his own hands and feet to restore their limbs and joints.
Furthermore, by the power of his true and great vow, he caused that person’s body and life to be fully restored as they were before.

"By this most supreme root of goodness, may I achieve the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; I shall then bestow the flavor of the Dharma upon that person, ultimately causing them to abide in the peace and bliss of Nirvana."
When this vow was made, the entire great earth shook in six ways, and the celestial palace of Śakra was likewise shaken and alerted.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, reflected to himself:
"What kind of omen is this?"
He further observed and saw that Prince Puṇyabala was performing those most supreme and extremely difficult deeds; he rejoiced and marveled at them.
He then thought:
"Now this one of great majesty performs such a difficult task; what is it that he seeks?"
"I should now go to verify the reason for this.
He immediately transformed his appearance into that of a brahmin, descended from the heavens, and stood before the prince, saying: "Prince!
"I have previously seen you cut off your own hands and feet; for what purpose did you do so?
The Prince replied, "O Benevolent One!"
"The suffering of others is my own suffering;
the happiness of others is my own happiness.

Therefore, when I previously saw a person being punished who was in great agony, by the power of truth, I sacrificed my own hands, feet, and limbs to fill and restore the places where his body had been severed. Through the sincerity of that vow, he was restored to his former state."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was even more filled with admiration and wonder; he immediately resumed his original form and addressed the Prince, saying:
"Is it not because of a lack of sincerity, or because you seek something else, or because you have regressed, that you would abandon your own body?"
The Prince replied:
"Lord of Devas!
In my relinquishing my own hands and feet, there was no lack of sincerity, nor was there any ulterior motive, nor was there any turning back."
Śakra spoke again:
"If it be so, how may I be made to verify this matter?
The Prince replied:
"O Lord of Devas!
Have you not heard that all that I do is by the power of truth?
Thereupon, the Prince gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; observing the four quarters with the power of his true vow, he spoke this verse:
“If what I have spoken is true— that I am bound by the fetter of craving for my own body—
and that at this very moment I do not waver from the truth, may this body of mine become as it was before.”
"Having spoken these verses, the Prince’s limbs were immediately restored to their former state.
Consequently, celestial flowers rained down everywhere from the sky, celestial music—subtle, exquisite, and delightful—was played, a gentle breeze arose, and various auspicious signs appeared."
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Puṇyabala, Volume Two.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Puṇyabala, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Dharma Master, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Shi Hu, and others, by imperial decree:

"At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beheld these signs of merit, the karmic fruits manifested in this life, and these rare and auspicious portents; furthermore, knowing that both humans and devas were all filled with joy, he was greatly moved in his heart."
He then said to Prince Puṇyabala: "Prince!
Since you are now so diligently cultivating such supreme practices, what is it that you seek?"
The Prince replied,
"Lord of Devas!

I seek to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death, and to cause them all to abide securely in ultimate *nirvāṇa*."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that Prince Puṇyabala was diligently seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi with a profound resolve as immovable as Mount Sumeru, approved of his intention and spoke these words of praise:
"Excellent, excellent!
"O Mahāsattva!
You possess a vast and supreme power of aspiration; you shall certainly and swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having spoken thus, he vanished from sight.

"Furthermore, later on, the king of that country passed away at an advanced age. Before the king had yet installed his consecrated crown prince, the royal kinsmen, ministers, and subjects gathered for a council and said:
'Who among us should now be made to succeed to the position of consecrated ruler?'"
Then one person said, "If there is one of great merit and high renown, he should be worthy to succeed to the throne.
After these words were spoken, the assembly was of one mind; they immediately dispatched messengers to travel everywhere in search of him.

"At that time, Prince Puṇyabala, who was to succeed to the royal throne, had his roots of goodness fully developed; accompanied by his attendants, he went out to stroll through the gardens and groves.
As the prince traveled, the roads were level, and at every point there were no thorns, pebbles, or gravel.
Along the way, auspicious signs appeared:"
Fine rain scattered from the sky, swirling and spreading above his head;
birds of extraordinary colors circled gracefully in succession;
boys and girls emitted sublime sounds, leaping and rushing about, all filled with joy.
The body hairs of all the people stood on end with joy, and they all attained physical and mental ease.
Furthermore, they heard pleasing words from the air.
Upon witnessing these signs, the Prince immediately gave rise to this thought:
"Since these signs have appeared, I shall certainly succeed to the position of consecration.
Having formed this thought, he proceeded to the park and enjoyed various blessings and pleasures.
In that garden there was a great *aśoka* tree, its flowers in full and lush bloom; the Prince lay sleeping peacefully beneath it.
Those who had gone with him, desiring the flowers and fruits, each wandered and enjoyed themselves throughout the garden at their various leisure spots.

Furthermore, by the power of the Prince’s merit, a nāga king suddenly caused a thousand-petaled, exquisite lotus flower to spring up from the earth; it was vast in size, perfect in color and fragrance, and most supremely lovely.
Then that Dragon King, by means of his supernormal power, gently placed the Prince upon a lotus flower;
at that time, the Prince was entirely without movement or sensation.

As the mealtime gradually passed and the sun reached its zenith, the shadows of all other trees shifted, yet only the shadow of the Ashoka tree remained covering the Prince’s body, as before, without moving.
Furthermore, all the other flowering trees within that grove leaned toward the great Aśoka tree, which possessed auspicious and supreme characteristics and was pleasing and beautiful to behold.

At that time, Prince Puṇyabala saw in a dream that he was situated upon filth; he also saw himself stained by filth; he saw himself licking the sky with his tongue; he saw himself standing in the midst of a lotus flower; he saw himself rising up to the peaks of mountains; and he saw a multitude of people prostrating themselves before him.
Having awakened, the Prince examined his dream according to its significance as follows:
"That I saw myself standing upon filth in my dream signifies that I shall certainly occupy the position of a consecrated king, possessing great wealth and sovereignty; this was the preceding omen."
As I perceive those whose bodies are defiled by impurities, I should occupy the great lion throne.
As I perceive those who rise above like mountain peaks, I should always abide at the highest point in all places.
"As I observe that the multitude prostrates before me, I ought to be honored by this assembly.
Having carefully examined such signs as these, I am now certain that I shall become a consecrated king."

At that time, the ministers and officials of that kingdom first dispatched messengers to travel throughout the land in search of him; they arrived at the garden and beheld the Prince’s successive and continuous marks of auspicious excellence.
Their hearts were struck with wonder, thinking: "This one possesses such great power of merit and such a vast reputation."
He immediately returned in haste and reported the aforementioned matters in detail.
Upon hearing his words, all the ministers and assistants were filled with joy.

They then prepared everything required according to the ritual protocols and proceeded to the garden to confer the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) upon him. Having arrived, they beheld various auspicious and excellent signs.
At that time, Prince Puṇyabala sat cross-legged upon a subtle and magnificent great lotus flower.

Because of the unfolding power of his merit, the Four Great Heavenly Kings offered a celestial, grandly adorned lion throne; Śakra, Lord of Devas, offered a celestial, exquisite parasol and various jeweled fly-whisks; and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven offered various precious ornaments for a pavilion, scattering myriad jewel flowers that descended like clouds.
The hosts of devaputras in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings rained down various jewels, played exquisite and delightful celestial music, and scattered wonderful garments.
The groves and gardens throughout the land were completely pure, entirely free of thorns, gravel, or pebbles.

Banners and streamers were erected and draped with interlacing strings of pearls and silk; exquisite incense vases were set out, and various extraordinary flowers were scattered until it equaled a celestial palace.

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, commanded the devaputra Viśvakarman to cause vast, multi-storied pavilions made of the four precious substances to manifest throughout the gardens, so that the Prince might enjoy them at his pleasure.

At that time, the ministers and attendants, beholding such rare and extraordinary signs, were moved even further to wonder; all with solemn reverence, they respectfully commanded the Crown Prince to occupy the lion throne, prostrating themselves in veneration and honoring him according to the prescribed rites by conferring upon him the consecration.
Once the Prince had received the consecration, light issued from his body, illuminating everything within a distance of one *yojana*, so that even the sunlight was eclipsed and no longer appeared.
At that time, among the assembly, there was one group of people who, having seen this light, all exclaimed:
"This is King Śuddhodana.
Another group of people said:
"This is King Puṇyabala.

At that time, as King Puṇyabala was about to enter the royal city, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the others, having performed offerings before the king according to the prescribed rites, vanished back to their celestial palaces.

When King Puṇyabala had entered the city, he administered state affairs with great skill; the population flourished, and the realm was peaceful, secure, and prosperous. All strife and contention were stilled, and external enemies were repelled. There were no longer any thieves, famines, or diseases, and he cherished his people as if they were his only son.

The groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees were all in full bloom and lush; the seasons did not fail, the harvests were abundant, the rains fell in their proper time, and the great earth was moistened by their nourishment.

Furthermore, subsequently, the four elder brothers of the king heard of this extraordinary event and were all struck with wonder and astonishment. They deliberated together, saying: "Prince Puṇyabala surpasses us;

he is complete in both merit and wisdom. By the power of his merit, he has become a great king and possesses supreme wealth, which accords with our hearts' desire. At this time, we ought to go to him together."
Thereupon, the four elder brothers went together to the place where King Puṇyabala was.
Having arrived, they immediately addressed him with these words:
"May you, O Most Victorious One, increase in longevity."
Again, he praised him, saying: "Excellent,
Great King!"

"Your former vow has now been firmly established; with such merit and wisdom, you surpass us and shall preside over the great throne as king in another land—all of which is accomplished through the power of your superior merit."
"Our kinsmen and friends have all witnessed this together.

Then, King Puṇyabala descended joyfully from his lion throne, paid his respects, and inquired after their welfare. He then prepared high and spacious seats as was appropriate and bade his elder brothers take their places in order.
The elder brothers then commanded the King to resume his seat.
Once the assembly was settled, they presented various offerings.
After discussing the matters previously debated, they all gave rise to a heart of resolute joy.
At that time, the king gave rise to a sense of reverence and each offered what they had brought.
After such an assembly had lasted two or three days, the king instructed his brothers and the gathered multitude, causing them to understand the nature of merit and demerit, and spoke these verses:
"Those without merit fall into hell, Where they undergo great suffering and torment without interruption."
Some fall among the hungry ghosts or as animals, suffering from hunger, thirst, and the burden of heavy loads.
Those without merit have their bodies ruined; those without merit become slaves, exhausted by extreme toil.
Those without merit fall into the state of being deaf or mute; those without merit are dull-witted and possessed of much perverse wisdom.
Those without merit are possessed by malevolent spirits; those without merit have ugly forms.
Those without merit are mostly born into lowly clans; those without merit have disordered minds and are loathed by others.
Those without merit are often deluded; those without merit are slighted and slandered by others.
Whatever one who lacks merit undertakes, though they exert themselves with diligence, it will not succeed.
The body of one who lacks merit is coarse and rough; entirely devoid of majestic radiance, it is displeasing to behold.
Even the trees and grasses where a person lacking merit dwells become withered and parched, though once lush and green.
Those who lack merit are not followed by others, and external circumstances likewise cause them harm;
various evil spirits, rākṣasas, and piśācas constantly harass those devoid of merit.
When those without merit take medicine to treat an illness, it becomes instead a non-medicine and the disease intensifies;
because they lack merit, they suffer poverty and are further treated with contempt by others.
Those without merit who father children will have offspring of coarse and evil nature whom the multitude detests;
though those without merit may have many kinsmen, they are constantly separated from them, giving rise to suffering and distress.
Those without merit have their eyes impaired, and furthermore, a succession of various sufferings arises;
many illnesses stem from the cause of lacking merit, and minor ailments are indeed difficult to cure.
Those without merit are often fierce and evil; those without merit constantly utter coarse and harsh sounds.
Their fingers are clenched into fists and their bodies are incomplete; the words they speak are seldom believed or followed by others.
Whatever possessions a person without merit may have are consumed by kings, officials, water, fire, and thieves;
lacking merit, they hear only unpleasant words and are constantly filled with fear wherever they go.
Though one may dwell on level ground, if lacking merit, thorns will sprout wherever one goes;
even if one engages in planting or commerce, though one acts much, it will often yield no benefit.
For those without merit, at all times, all their wealth and treasures are scattered and destroyed;
they have not the slightest sense of attachment to the world, which is truly unlovely and devoid of benefit.
Such are the characteristics of those without merit; the wise should know that all such things are ruined.
The fortunate one protects the good they have performed, so that at all times it is never lost.
The fortunate one acts without weariness, always giving rise to a firm and courageous mind;
like a canopy providing vast and boundless shade, they are further able to ward off and eliminate the rain of all evils.
Just as a calf follows its mother and is constantly nourished by her milk, so too do those with merit find their noble desires fulfilled according to their wishes;
and like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) that delights the eye, they constantly obtain the fruits of all that they desire.
The fortunate one is able to possess the power of patience And attain delightful and great auspiciousness;
With faith and practice deep and firm to rely upon, In every birth they shall possess wondrous physical marks.
The fortunate one spreads a great reputation far and wide, possessing both extensive learning and wisdom;
all who behold him give rise to a heart of love and joy, and he further attains the power of hearing, retaining, and recollecting.
The fortunate one faces death without illness; at the time of death, they likewise give rise to joy.
Most evil signs do not appear before them, and they remain far removed from terror and suffering.
The fortunate one, at the moment of death, experiences celestial bliss; celestial palaces and towers appear before them.
Devas from the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens come one after another to welcome and escort them;
so too do the sons of the gods in the Tuṣita heaven and the hosts of the Nirmāṇarati heaven.
The gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven of the Desire Realm all come to protect the one who possesses merit.
That meritorious person is like the Great Brahmā King; ten million celestial hosts all revere him.
Within his thousand Brahma-worlds, he is vast, supreme, and sovereign.
One whose merit is such that all undertakings succeed, who constantly dwells in a state of happiness,
and for whom all beings conceive feelings of love and joy, shall remain unharmed even by external circumstances.
At that time, having heard the verses, the elder brothers and their retinue were all inspired with faith and submission toward King Puṇyabala, and they were filled with the utmost joy.
"In this life and in future lives, he clearly reveals and elucidates all things with complete knowledge; his power of merit is most supreme.
At that time, King Puṇyabala, having extensively explained the matters of merit to the great multitude and awakened their minds, gazed into the void and thought to himself:
"How wonderful! How joyful!"
"I can now cause all kinds of precious jewels and garments to rain down everywhere, both inside and outside the royal city.

As soon as he gave rise to this thought, various exquisite garments, pleasing flowers, and wonderful precious jewels suddenly descended from the heavens, completely filling the interior and exterior of the royal city.

When this sign appeared, humans and devas were all filled with joy; they were all struck with wonder and astonishment, and everyone gave rise to a heart of vast and pure faith, simultaneously exclaiming:
"How wonderful! How marvelous!"
"O Son of Heaven, he possesses such power of merit and is endowed with great majesty and virtue.
Furthermore, after the various minor kings heard of these matters, they all gave rise to this thought:
"That king possesses great power of merit and is endowed with great renown; we should now go to him to pay our respects and offer our service."

"Thereupon, the kings assembled in one place; each leading his fourfold army—namely, the elephant, cavalry, chariot, and infantry divisions—they proceeded together to the abode of King Puṇyabala. Alighting from their vehicles, they advanced forward, paid obeisance with solemn reverence, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
'Your Majesty possesses great merit and great renown; as a great king, your majesty and virtue are preeminent. We have now come specifically to pay our respects to you in person.'"

Then King Puṇyabala again addressed his inquiries and offered universal consolation. Once they had sat down in order, he bestowed priceless and most excellent precious jewels upon each of them, along with their respective officials and retinues;
furthermore, he universally gathered and transformed them through the gateway of the ten virtuous dharmas.
At that time, all the kings attained victory and each returned to their own country.

Furthermore, subsequently, King Balacakṣus heard of these extraordinary events through successive reports; he first dispatched envoys to that kingdom, and then, accompanied by his officials and attendants, he himself proceeded with great speed, pressing forward day and night without ceasing.

When the Father King arrived, out of his deep affection for his son, he saw him from afar; his eyes brimmed with tears as sorrow and joy mingled within him. With a piteous voice and a heart full of longing, he quickly descended from his chariot, went forward, and took hold of his son's hand.

Gazing at him for a long time, the Father King then said: "I am your father, as you surely know well. I am now old and decrepit like this; the governance of the kingdom is extremely difficult, and I am no longer capable of bearing its burden. I now entrust it to you; you must take up this responsibility."
Having spoken thus, he immediately removed his own jeweled crown and placed it upon the head of his son. Following his father’s instruction, the son governed the kingdom concurrently with him.
The Sūtra on the因缘 (nidāna) of Prince Puṇyabala, Scroll Three.
The Sūtra on the因缘 (nidāna) of Prince Puṇyabala, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma-transmitting Master and Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Shi Hu, et al., under Imperial Decree:

"Furthermore, King Puṇyabala exercised sovereign governance throughout the entire realm of Jambudvīpa; his nation was wealthy and he possessed absolute power, his majesty and virtue being preeminent."
The king provided all the people with an abundance of precious treasures and wealth, universally guiding them through the ten wholesome dharmas.

At that time, the people of Jambudvīpa flourished, lived in peace and happiness, ceased all strife, and repelled external enemies; there were no thieves, famines, or epidemics, nor was there anyone who was impoverished, infirm, or disabled.
All possess treasuries and storehouses filled with wealth and jewels, with vast retinues and sovereign mastery as they desire.
Furthermore, in all directions and locations, thorns, brambles, sand, and gravel are naturally removed.
The seasons proceeded without fail, and the rains were abundant and nourishing; flowers and fruits flourished, and the harvests were bountiful.

The people all recognized that the power of merit had increased and surpassed its former state; they constantly practiced giving and performed various meritorious deeds, purifying themselves and clarifying their minds as they cultivated the observance of the precepts.
When those in Jambudvīpa reach the end of their lives, they are all reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;

King Puṇyabala extensively developed the roots of goodness for countless multitudes, bringing great benefit in both the present life and future existences, such that thousands of people reached the end of their lives and were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know this: who else could that King Puṇyabala have been?
It was none other than myself; at that time, I was dwelling in the stage of a bodhisattva."
The King of Eye-Power, father of King Puṇyabala, was the present King Śuddhodana.
Queen Vistīrṇaprabhā was the present Lady Māyā.
The youth endowed with perfect physical marks was the present Bhikṣu Ānanda.
The youth endowed with diligence is now the bhikṣu Śrutaviṃśatikoṭi;
the youth endowed with craftsmanship is now the bhikṣu Aniruddha.
The youth endowed with wisdom was the bhikṣu Śāriputra at that time;
the Lord of the Devas, Śakra, was the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana at that time.
The king who passed away was none other than Māra, the King of Maras.
The poor man was the bhikṣu Rāhula.
The skilled physician who administered the punishment was the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya.
"O Bhikṣus!
For this reason, you should know the power of merit; therefore, at all times, all sentient beings should extensively cultivate and perform all superior karmic actions."
"Therefore, when I previously spoke of that power of merit, I did not see even the slightest dharma which, once practiced and cultivated, would yield such great benefit.
At that time, all the bhikṣus conceived doubts and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

What kind of karmic practices did that King Puṇyabala cultivate in ages past to bring about such a retribution—that he rules over all kingdoms, possesses great renown, is preeminent in majestic virtue, and enjoys the blessings of devas and humans; that whatever he requires appears as soon as he thinks of it, descending from the heavens; that at his birth the earth shook, precious jewels rained from the sky, and a lion throne descended; and that Śakra offered him a parasol, a treasure-vault appeared, and so forth? How is this so?
"I pray that the Buddha will resolve this.
The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣus!"

King Puṇyabala had accumulated and cultivated meritorious deeds throughout successive lifetimes; through the convergence of the power of his vast vows and conditions, he was destined to receive a superior karmic reward of merit accordingly.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!

You should know that all karmic actions performed by sentient beings cannot be obtained through external conditions, nor are they produced by the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Whether wholesome or unwholesome, these various karmic actions arise in accordance with the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).
He then spoke these verses:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, the causes of various karmas do not perish;
when the conditions and causes converge, sentient beings experience their fruits accordingly."

“O Bhikṣus! I recall that in the distant past, long ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Aśoka (Invincible) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

Having universally performed the work of a Buddha throughout the world, that Buddha finally entered the realm of great nirvana without remainder in a single kingdom, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
The king of that country collected the relics and erected a precious stūpa, making vast offerings to them.

Subsequently, the community of bhikṣus sounded the *gaṇḍī*, beat drums, and blew conch shells to announce to the great assembly. At that time, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus gathered in one place, and on an auspicious day, that great Dharma master extensively proclaimed the essential points of the Dharma for all the people.

At that time, there was a gambler in the kingdom named Deśena (Victorious), who was deeply addicted to games of chance, board games, and other diversions; his wife was named Viśākhā (Extensive Victory), and his son was also named the same.

This man had previously accumulated family wealth, but because of his addiction to gambling, he lost all his internal and external possessions to others until they were entirely dissipated; he now possesses nothing but two pieces of cotton cloth he wears, the parasol he always carries, a pair of leather sandals, and five gold coins.
At one time, that man suddenly said:
"I did not perform meritorious deeds; it is because of this that I suffer such poverty.
Having spoken, he sighed deeply, took the aforementioned items, and immediately left his house to seek out places for gambling in succession.

When he arrived at the place where the Dharma was being taught, he saw the Great Dharma Master seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a multitude of people who stood with palms joined, listening to the Dharma.
Upon beholding this sublime sight, the man gave rise to a pure mind and thought to himself:
"I, too, shall now listen to the Dharma here."
He immediately set aside all his belongings in one place and, with palms joined in reverent sincerity, listened to what was being said.
At that time, the Dharma Master spoke these verses:
"One should cultivate the causes of all merits; Just as they have been performed, let them not be interrupted."
"When one acts according to one's desires, One obtains sublime bliss by virtue of a treasury of merit.
Having heard this verse, that person reflected on its meaning:

"If one obtains sublime bliss by virtue of a treasury of merit, then because I failed to create meritorious causes during my previous lives, I have come to experience poverty and suffering. I should now, according to my ability, perform even a small amount of meritorious deeds."
He then reflected to himself:
"My family wealth has been entirely dissipated; now I have nothing but these personal belongings.
If I were to take five gold coins and a piece of cotton cloth from among them to practice giving, I fear that such extreme poverty would lead to the loss of my life."
If one does not practice giving, the causes for merit will be forever destroyed, and in future lives there will be no place of refuge.
By what means can I now escape the suffering of poverty and sustain my life, while practicing meritorious deeds so as not to ruin these superior causes?
"However, I would rather endure hunger and poverty now than fail to cultivate meritorious deeds; it is fitting that I should give these gold coins and cotton garments as offerings.
While he was thinking this, the Dharma Master spoke these verses:
"One should swiftly cultivate wholesome dharmas, For they can immediately extinguish all sinful karma."
"In this way, one should cultivate the causes of supreme merit; all sinful karma is not to be desired.

Having heard these verses, that person reflected deeply on their words: "One must swiftly cultivate wholesome dharmas"—this was his firm resolve. Thereupon, he gave rise to a mind of pure generosity: he took the parasol he held and covered the head of the Dharma Master; he took his leather sandals and placed them at the Master's feet; he scattered five gold coins beside the seat; and he lifted a piece of cotton cloth and draped it over the Dharma Master’s body.
With his heart filled with great joy and the hairs on his body standing on end, he prostrated at [the Buddha’s] feet, his pure faith increasing further, and made this aspiration:

"By virtue of this supreme root of goodness from my gift of the Dharma, may I, from this life onward and in every subsequent birth, possess great and extraordinary power of merit, attain great renown, and enjoy the blessings of devas and humans. May my majestic virtue be preeminent as I rule over all kingdoms; whatever I require shall appear the moment I think of it, and through the arising of excellent signs, may I obtain inexhaustible treasuries."
After he had made such vast aspirations, the Dharma Master then dedicated the merit accordingly.
At that time, the gambler departed from the assembly; wearing only a single garment to cover his body, he returned to his home.
At that time, when the wife and son saw this, they were struck with wonder and thought, "The various items previously held must have been dissipated through gambling while he was outside.
The wife then asked,
"O virtuous one!"
"In this house, only I and my son remain; there is nothing else left. Is it not the case that we too shall soon perish?
Because of this, that man’s distress increased further, and as he experienced the suffering of poverty, reflecting on these circumstances, he spoke these verses:
"What suffering in the world surpasses the suffering of poverty? For the suffering of poverty is equal to the suffering of death."
"I would rather endure the suffering of death with a willing heart than find pleasure in the suffering of poverty.
Having spoken these verses, he sighed deeply and remained silent.
Later, on one occasion, his wife took a jar to the well to draw water; although she reached the bottom and found water, her strength was insufficient to lift it out.
She then called her husband to witness this matter, and he immediately joined her in lifting it, yet they still could not bring it up.
She further summoned their son, and only when the three of them together exerted themselves with fierce vigor and great effort were they finally able to lift it slightly.
Puzzled, he looked down and saw beneath him five iron jars, filled to the brim with gold and arranged in a continuous row.
Having already been struck with wonder by his prior vision, he reflected: "Could this not be that what was previously bestowed has now yielded its fruit?"
Gazing with a joyful countenance, he spoke these verses:
"How marvelous! These merits have manifested here, And all faults have been entirely eliminated.
What is attained now arises from seeds sown in the past; Such is the fruit of the donor’s reward."
At that time, his wife asked with joy: "O Noble One!
Since your excellent marks are such as these and your eloquent speech is so wonderful, what is the reason for this?"
Thus he spoke, explaining the matter in detail as was appropriate.

Furthermore, at a later time, that victorious gambler’s power of merit manifested, and he immediately obtained this fruit. Consequently, his fame spread far and wide, and the people of the kingdom said to one another:
“How marvelous! How rare! By means of such extraordinary and great merit, he has suddenly attained great wealth and sovereignty.”

From that time forward, that person turned toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, developing a purity of faith far exceeding what they had before, and daily made extensive offerings at the stūpas of the Buddha.

Furthermore, he listened to and practiced the True Dharma; moreover, he daily provided the finest delicacies to the pure assembly as well as to other śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the destitute, and beggars, supplying them with all their necessary provisions according to their needs and ensuring they were fully satisfied.

Furthermore, he extensively constructed a monastery and invited monks from the four quarters to reside there, providing them with service and offerings; consequently, his fame spread throughout the cities and towns.

Later, that king suddenly passed away without an heir. At that time, the ministers and kinsmen, knowing full well that this man possessed great power of merit and a great reputation, deliberated together and earnestly requested him to succeed to the royal throne.
At that time, the gambler concealed his original name, and everyone addressed him as King Vijitāvin.

Having manifested such a delightful karmic reward, King Vijitāvin gave rise to a fierce and intense resolve; he excelled his previous generosity by performing various meritorious deeds and practicing the observance of the precepts. After the king had universally opened the causes of merit for his ministers, kinsmen, and all the people, he eventually reached the end of his life and was reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) as the son of its celestial king.

When one is born in that heaven, various supreme, exquisite, and pleasing precious jewels, as well as manifold garments and ornaments, descend from the sky. One’s own body possesses a radiance that outshines the radiance of the other celestial hosts so that it does not appear; when the gods of that heaven see this, they are all struck with wonder and exclaim, "How marvelous! Such is the fruit of superior merit!"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know this: who else could that King Jayasena have been?
It was none other than the King Puṇyabala previously mentioned."

At that time, he who was originally a gambler was able to give rise to a joyful mind and delight in hearing the Dharma; he exhausted all his possessions to bestow them upon the Dharma Master. Consequently, in this present life, he obtained a superior karmic retribution, succeeding to the royal throne and cultivating the causes of merit.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, he became the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven for twenty-six lifetimes, and the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven for thirty-six lifetimes.
For thirty-six births he was the King of the Tuṣita Heaven;
for thirty-six births he was the King of the Yāma Heaven;
for thirty-six births he was the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
For thirty-six lifetimes he was the Lord of the Four Great Kings;
for countless hundreds of lifetimes he was a Golden-Wheel-Turning King,
ruling and transforming the four continents with the True Dharma, fully endowed with the seven treasures.

That is to say, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure—these seven treasures he enjoys at will.

Furthermore, he has a thousand sons of supreme physical beauty, courageous, vigorous, and capable of subduing enemy armies. Throughout the entire realm of the great earth, reaching to the very limits of the ocean, there are no fears of thieves, weapons, or staves; all practice the True Dharma and dwell in peace and security.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣus:
“Such supreme causes as these, O Great Being, Lead to birth as a sovereign lord;
Because the Buddha universally gathers all within the world— This is what all Buddhas have proclaimed.”

If one hears of this rare occurrence, as well as these vast causes for such supernormal powers, even those who have committed black deeds will give rise to faith; who among the wise would not be awakened?
Therefore, such is this great rarity: that those of great majestic power grant whatever is sought;
one should revere the gateway of the True Dharma and constantly keep in mind the teachings of all Buddhas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“As I have taught, you should train yourselves in this way: always diligently love and delight in the True Dharma, honoring, respecting, faithfully upholding, and making offerings to it. Having acted thus, take it as your reliance; those who train in this manner will obtain great benefit.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Puṇyabala*, Scroll Four.
